annotations.keyFindings: A four-line medicines prompt was followed by a fall in handoffs with an omitted medication item from 41 to 22 percent over 16 weeks on two medical wards. Handoff took about 40 seconds longer per patient.
annotations.limitations: Uncontrolled before-after comparison on two wards of one hospital; reviewers knew the period; no measure of patient harm.

annotations.keyFindings: Moving handoff to the bedside was followed by about one third fewer pharmacist-found discrepancies, with no change on a comparison ward. Patients corrected a nurse's statement about their medicines in 6 percent of observed bedside handoffs.
annotations.limitations: One intervention ward; counts depend on pharmacist workload; a new electronic medication record arrived at the same time.

annotations.keyFindings: Fifteen of 19 studies found fewer omissions with a structured tool, most often in medication content. Effects were larger with audit and feedback; only three studies had a concurrent control.
annotations.limitations: Heterogeneous outcomes prevented pooling; most included studies at high risk of bias; search ended in 2021.

annotations.keyFindings: Checklist wards had 18 percent fewer handoffs with a missed medication item at three months, but the difference disappeared by seven months after feedback stopped, while completion fell from 85 to 52 percent.
annotations.limitations: Allocation by manager preference; unblinded outcome assessment; wide interval around a ward-level difference.

annotations.keyFindings: Patients valued hearing about their medicines; the 07:00 bedside handoff was sometimes intrusive and some asked to be skipped when asleep.
annotations.limitations: 24 patients from one hospital; conversations held by ward staff.

annotations.keyFindings: Handoff sheet review against the medication administration record found 81 percent of the missed items seen by direct observation, with good agreement between reviewers.
annotations.limitations: One ward and one observer pair.

annotations.keyFindings: Patients with hearing impairment took part in 31 percent and patients with cognitive impairment in 18 percent of bedside medicines discussions, against 64 percent of other awake patients.
annotations.limitations: Three wards of one hospital; participation judged by observers who knew the aim.

claims.text: On two medical wards, handoffs with at least one omitted medication item fell from 41 percent to 22 percent after a four-line medicines prompt was added to the handoff sheet.
claims.passage: handoffs with at least one omitted medication item fell from 41 percent to 22 percent
claims.interpretation: Supports a medicines section in the checklist; the design is uncontrolled, so the size of change is a planning value only.

claims.text: In a controlled evaluation on medical wards, the reduction in missed medication items was no longer visible at seven months once audit feedback had stopped.
claims.passage: Audit feedback stopped after the fourth month, and by seven months the difference was no longer visible.
claims.interpretation: Feedback belongs in the change package and checklist completion should be tracked.

claims.text: Review of written handoff sheets against the medication administration record found 81 percent of the missed items seen by direct observation.
claims.passage: Sheet review identified 81 percent of the missed items found by direct observation.
claims.interpretation: Sheet review is a workable data source for the run chart and misses about one item in five.

claims.text: Patients with hearing or cognitive impairment took part in bedside medicines discussions far less often than other awake patients.
claims.passage: Patients with hearing impairment took part in 31 percent of handoffs and patients with cognitive impairment in 18 percent, compared with 64 percent of other awake patients.
claims.interpretation: Report missed items separately for patients who cannot take part at the bedside.

synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. A medicines prompt in structured handoff was followed by fewer omitted medication items in a before-after study (41 to 22 percent), a time series and most studies in a systematic review, but the only concurrently controlled evaluation lost its effect by seven months once audit feedback stopped. Handoff sheet review against the medication administration record is a workable measurement method that misses about one item in five. Patients with hearing or cognitive impairment take part in bedside medicines discussions far less often. No study measured adverse drug events with adequate power. The evidence supports testing a checklist locally with run charts, feedback and balancing measures rather than assuming an effect size.
gradeRationale: Mostly uncontrolled or non-randomised comparisons from single sites, one review of heterogeneous studies at high risk of bias, and one controlled evaluation whose effect did not last; consistent direction but serious risk of bias. Certainty that a checklist reduces missed items is low; certainty about harm reduction is very low.
summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; four source-derived claims recorded with passages; overall certainty low.
